subject: chem
title: Stoichiometry
subtitle: Moles, empirical/molecular formulae, titrations and gas volumes.
concept: The mole links macroscopic mass to the number of particles. One mole contains 6.02×10²³ particles (Avogadro's constant).
Balanced equations give molar ratios — the key tool for all stoichiometric calculations.
Concentration, gas volumes (using molar volume 24 dm³ at RTP) and titration data all convert to moles for calculation.

notes.heading: The Mole and Molar Mass
items: The mole links the macroscopic world (grams you can weigh) to the microscopic world (individual atoms/molecules). One mole contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles — Avogadro's constant (Nₐ).
Molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance in g mol⁻¹; numerically equal to the relative molecular (or atomic) mass.
n = m / Mᵣ  — moles = mass (g) divided by molar mass (g mol⁻¹).

notes.heading: Concentration and Volume
items: n = c × V  where concentration c is in mol dm⁻³ and volume V must be in dm³ (divide cm³ by 1000).
At RTP (25 °C, 1 atm), the molar volume of any ideal gas is 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹. So n = V / 24.0.
For non-standard conditions: PV = nRT, where R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, P in Pa, V in m³, T in K.

notes.heading: Empirical and Molecular Formulae
items: Empirical formula: simplest whole-number ratio of atoms. Find it by dividing each element's % mass by its Aᵣ, then dividing all values by the smallest.
Molecular formula = (empirical formula) × n, where n = Mᵣ(molecular) / Mᵣ(empirical).
Combustion analysis: burn the compound; collect CO₂ (→ moles of C) and H₂O (→ moles of H); find O by mass difference.

notes.heading: Titration Calculations
items: Steps: calculate moles of the known solution → use the molar ratio from the balanced equation → find moles of unknown → calculate concentration or mass.
Back titration: add a measured excess of reagent A to the sample; titrate the remaining excess against reagent B; subtract to find how much A reacted with the sample.
Standard solution: a solution of accurately known concentration made from a primary standard (e.g. anhydrous Na₂CO₃).

notes.heading: Percentage Yield and Atom Economy
items: % yield = (actual moles of product / theoretical moles) × 100. The theoretical yield assumes complete reaction with no losses.
Atom economy = (Mᵣ of desired product / sum of Mᵣ of all products) × 100. A high atom economy means less waste — greener chemistry.
Addition reactions have 100% atom economy (only one product formed).

definitions.body: The amount of substance containing 6.02×10²³ particles (Avogadro's constant).
The mass of one mole of a substance, in g mol⁻¹; numerically equal to the relative molecular mass.
The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.
The percentage of the total mass of reactants that becomes the desired product: (Mr desired product / ΣMr all products) × 100.
A solution of accurately known concentration, prepared from a primary standard.

workedExamples.q: A compound contains 40.0% C, 6.7% H and 53.3% O by mass. Its Mr = 60. Find the molecular formula.

steps.text: C:1, H:2, O:1 → empirical formula CH₂O, Mr = 30

workedExamples.q: 25.0 cm³ of H₂SO₄ requires 30.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH to reach the endpoint. Find [H₂SO₄].

mistakes: Using cm³ instead of dm³ in concentration calculations — always divide cm³ by 1000.
Forgetting to use the molar ratio from the balanced equation before finding concentration.
Confusing empirical formula (simplest ratio) with molecular formula (actual number of atoms).
tips: Write out the full equation and mark the molar ratio before substituting numbers.
In combustion analysis, find C from CO₂ (1 mol CO₂ → 1 mol C), H from H₂O (1 mol H₂O → 2 mol H), then O by difference.
Atom economy favours reactions where only one product forms — addition reactions have 100% atom economy.
